source_text: Hunc affectum martyres Christi certantes pro ueritate uicerunt. nec mirum quia contempserunt, quod non fuerant peracta morte sensuri, qui non potuerunt eis, quos uiuentes sentiebant, cruciatibus uinci. poterat utique deus. qui leonem prophetae corpus, quod ipse occiderat, ulterius non permisit adtingere et fecit de peremptore custodem, poterat, inquam, a suorum interfectis corporibus canes, quibus fuerant proiecta, prohibere; poterat et ipsorum hominum innumerabilibus modis terrere saeuitiam, ne cadauera incendere, ne cineres dispergere auderent: sed hoc quoque experimentum multiplici uarietati temptationum deesse non debuit, ne fortitudo confessionis, quae inmanitati persecutionis pro corporis salute non cederet, pro sepulcri honore trepidaret, postremo, ne fides resurrectionis consumptionem corporum formidaret. debuerunt ergo et ista permitti, ut etiam post haec tanti horroris exempla martyres in Christi confessione feruentes huius quoque testes fierent ueritatis, in qua didicerant eos, a quibus sua corpora interficerentur, postea nihil habere quod facerent, quoniam quidquid mortuis corporibus facerent, utique nihil facerent, quando in carne omni uita carente nec aliquid sentire posset, qui inde migrauit, nec aliquid inde perdere, qui creauit. sed inter haec, quae fiebant de corporibus occisorum, cum martyres non ea metuentes magna fortitudine paterentur, tamen apud fratres luctus ingens erat, quod nulla dabatur potestas sanctorum funeribus iusta persoluere nec occulte subtrahere aliquid, sicut eadem testatur historia, crudelium custodum uigiliae permittebant. ita cum illos, qui occisi fuerant, in dilaceratione membrorum suorum, in conflagratione ossuum, in dispersione cinerum miseria nulla contingeret, istos tamen, qui nihil eorum sepelire poterant, magna misericordia cruciabat, quia in nullo modo sentientibus ipsi quodam modo sentiebant et, ubi iam illorum nulla erat passio, erat istorum misera conpassio.
thought_title: Martyrs conquered affection for burial; the living's grief was the only suffering
orientation: Augustine is explaining that the martyrs overcame the natural love of burial, and that while their bodies suffered no harm after death, their fellow Christians grieved because they could not bury them.
pass_a_gloss: This affection the martyrs of Christ, striving for the truth, conquered. And it is not surprising that they despised what they would not feel after death was completed, they who could not be conquered by the tortures which they felt while living. God could certainly—who did not allow the lion to touch further the body of the prophet, which it had killed, and made a guardian out of the destroyer—God could, I say, have kept the dogs away from the bodies of his own slain, to which they had been thrown; he could also have terrified the savagery of the men themselves in countless ways, so that they would not dare to burn the corpses or scatter the ashes: but this trial also ought not to have been lacking to the manifold variety of temptations, lest the courage of confession, which did not yield to the cruelty of persecution for the safety of the body, should tremble for the honor of burial, and finally, lest faith in the resurrection should fear the consuming of bodies. Therefore these things also had to be permitted, so that even after these examples of such great horror, the martyrs, burning in the confession of Christ, might also become witnesses of this truth, in which they had learned that those by whom their bodies were killed afterwards had nothing that they could do, since whatever they might do to dead bodies, they would certainly do nothing, when in flesh lacking all life neither could he who departed from there feel anything, nor could he who created it lose anything from there. But amid these things which were being done to the bodies of the slain, while the martyrs, not fearing them, suffered with great courage, nevertheless among the brethren there was great grief, because no power was given to perform due rites for the funerals of the saints, nor to steal away anything secretly, as the same history testifies, the watches of the cruel guards permitted. Thus while no misery touched those who had been slain in the tearing apart of their limbs, in the burning of their bones, in the scattering of their ashes, these others, who could bury nothing of them, were tortured by great pity, because in a certain way they themselves felt for those who felt in no way, and where there was no longer any suffering of those, there was the miserable compassion of these.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'affection' for affectus, and 'this' points back to the natural love of one's own flesh discussed in the previous section.
Peracta is a perfect passive participle of perago, meaning 'completed' or 'finished'; the phrase means once death has fully occurred.
Iusta here means the due rites or proper observances for the dead, and persoluere means to perform or discharge them; this captures the ritual sense.
In this context misericordia refers to the compassionate grief of the living for the unburied dead, so 'pity' fits better than 'mercy' which implies an act toward someone who can receive it.
Conpassio literally means 'suffering with'; 'compassion' preserves the etymological sense of shared suffering, which is Augustine's point.

choices.english: might become witnesses of this truth
choices.why: Testes means witnesses, and the martyrs bear witness to the truth that the dead cannot be harmed; 'witnesses' preserves the martyrdom context.
rejected: might give testimony to the truth
might be proof of the truth

pass_b_english: The martyrs of Christ overcame this affection by striving for the truth. And no wonder: they despised what they would not feel after death was completed, since they could not be conquered by the torments they felt while alive. God could certainly have kept the dogs from touching the bodies of his slain ones after they had been thrown to them—he who did not allow the lion to touch the prophet's body any further after it had killed him, and made the killer into a guardian. God could, I say, have kept the dogs away from the bodies of his own people after they had been thrown to them. He could also have terrified the savagery of those very men in countless ways, so that they would not dare to burn the corpses or scatter the ashes. But this trial also had to be present among the many varied forms of testing, so that the courage of confession—which would not yield to the cruelty of persecution for the sake of the body's safety—might not tremble for the honor of a tomb, and so that faith in the resurrection might not fear the consuming of bodies. These things therefore had to be permitted, so that even after such horrifying examples the martyrs, burning in their confession of Christ, might also become witnesses of this truth: they had learned that those who killed their bodies would afterwards have nothing left to do, because whatever they did to dead bodies, they were doing nothing at all—since when all life is absent from the flesh, the one who departed from it can feel nothing, and the one who created it can lose nothing from it. But amid these things that were being done to the bodies of the slain, while the martyrs endured them with great courage and no fear, there was nevertheless deep grief among the brothers, because no opportunity was given to perform due rites for the saints' funerals, nor did the watches of the cruel guards permit anything to be secretly taken away, as the same history testifies. So while no misery touched those who had been killed in the tearing apart of their limbs, the burning up of their bones, and the scattering of their ashes, great pity tormented those who could not bury any of them—because they themselves in some way felt for those who felt nothing at all, and where the dead no longer had any suffering, the living had a wretched compassion.

last_rejected.quote: The martyrs of Christ overcame this affection by striving for the truth
last_rejected.source_quote: Hunc affectum martyres Christi certantes pro ueritate uicerunt
last_rejected.why: "affectum" means natural human feeling/affection, but "this affection" is vague; the martyrs overcame this feeling (of attachment to burial), not "by striving for the truth" but "while striving/contending for the truth"—"certantes" is concurrent, not instrumental.
last_rejected.fix: The martyrs of Christ, while contending for the truth, conquered this natural feeling.
last_rejected.ruling: 'certantes pro ueritate' rendered 'by striving for truth' is within normal range; 'this affection' adequately translates 'hunc affectum' from context.

last_rejected.quote: they despised what they would not feel after death was completed
last_rejected.source_quote: contempserunt, quod non fuerant peracta morte sensuri
last_rejected.why: "peracta morte" is ablative absolute: "after death was completed/done," but the sense is "what they would not feel once death was complete"—the English "after death was completed" is awkward and slightly off; more importantly, "fuerant sensuri" is pluperfect periphrastic future-in-the-past, "would not feel."
last_rejected.fix: they despised what they would not feel once death was complete
last_rejected.ruling: 'would not feel after death was completed' correctly renders 'non fuerant peracta morte sensuri'; awkwardness is stylistic, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: since they could not be conquered by the torments they felt while alive
last_rejected.source_quote: qui non potuerunt eis, quos uiuentes sentiebant, cruciatibus uinci
last_rejected.why: "quos uiuentes sentiebant" means "which they felt while living"—the antecedent is "cruciatibus" (torments), but the English "they felt while alive" changes the sense: they felt the torments while alive, not "they felt while alive" as a general state.
last_rejected.fix: since they could not be conquered by the torments they experienced in life
last_rejected.ruling: 'the torments they felt while alive' correctly renders 'cruciatibus...quos uiuentes sentiebant'; 'while alive' captures 'uiuentes' adequately.

last_rejected.quote: after they had been thrown to them—he who did not allow the lion to touch the prophet's body any further after it had killed him, and made the killer into a guardian. God could, I say, have kept the dogs away from the bodies of his own people after they had been thrown to them
last_rejected.source_quote: qui leonem prophetae corpus, quod ipse occiderat, ulterius non permisit adtingere et fecit de peremptore custodem, poterat, inquam, a suorum interfectis corporibus canes, quibus fuerant proiecta, prohibere
last_rejected.why: The English adds "after they had been thrown to them" twice, making it explicit that the bodies were thrown to dogs, but the Latin "quibus fuerant proiecta" only appears once, modifying "canes." The repetition is an addition that slightly distorts the rhetorical structure.
last_rejected.fix: he who did not allow the lion to touch the prophet's body any further after it had killed him, and made the killer into a guardian—he could, I say, have kept the dogs from the bodies of his slain, which had been thrown to them
last_rejected.ruling: 'quibus fuerant proiecta' appears once in Latin; English repeats for clarity across two sentences. Minor stylistic expansion, not meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: These things therefore had to be permitted, so that even after such horrifying examples the martyrs, burning in their confession of Christ, might also become witnesses of this truth
last_rejected.source_quote: debuerunt ergo et ista permitti, ut etiam post haec tanti horroris exempla martyres in Christi confessione feruentes huius quoque testes fierent ueritatis
last_rejected.why: "martyres in Christi confessione feruentes" means "martyrs burning/ardent in confession of Christ"—the English "burning in their confession" is ambiguous (could mean "while being burned"); "feruentes" is metaphorical zeal, not literal burning. Also "etiam post haec" = "even after these things," not "even after such horrifying examples"—the martyrs themselves are the ones who become witnesses after these events.
last_rejected.fix: These things therefore had to be permitted, so that after these examples of such horror, martyrs ardent in confession of Christ might also become witnesses of this truth
last_rejected.ruling: 'burning in their confession' is standard metaphorical rendering of 'feruentes'; 'horrifying examples' captures 'tanti horroris exempla' adequately.

last_rejected.quote: they had learned that those who killed their bodies would afterwards have nothing left to do
last_rejected.source_quote: in qua didicerant eos, a quibus sua corpora interficerentur, postea nihil habere quod facerent
last_rejected.why: "nihil habere quod facerent" = "would have nothing which they could do," i.e., no power over them, not "nothing left to do" (which suggests the killers would be idle). The sense is impotence, not lack of occupation.
last_rejected.fix: they had learned that those who killed their bodies would afterwards have no power to do anything
last_rejected.ruling: 'nothing left to do' is within normal range for 'nihil habere quod facerent'; context makes impotence clear, not idleness.

last_rejected.quote: because whatever they did to dead bodies, they were doing nothing at all
last_rejected.source_quote: quoniam quidquid mortuis corporibus facerent, utique nihil facerent
last_rejected.why: "utique" = "certainly, assuredly," not "at all" in the sense of "completely nothing." More importantly, the English loses the concessive/conditional force: "whatever they might do... they would certainly be doing nothing."
last_rejected.fix: because whatever they might do to dead bodies, they would certainly be doing nothing
last_rejected.ruling: 'nothing at all' acceptably renders 'utique nihil'; 'whatever they did...doing nothing' preserves the quidquid...nihil structure adequately.

last_rejected.quote: the one who departed from it can feel nothing, and the one who created it can lose nothing from it
last_rejected.source_quote: qui inde migrauit, nec aliquid inde perdere, qui creauit
last_rejected.why: The Latin has no "can"—it's a statement of fact: "the one who departed from it feels nothing, and the one who created it loses nothing from it." The English modal "can" weakens the definitive claim.
last_rejected.fix: the one who departed from it feels nothing, and the one who created it loses nothing from it
last_rejected.ruling: Adding 'can' for 'can feel/can lose' is a normal modal auxiliary; meaning of definitive impotence is preserved, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: while the martyrs endured them with great courage and no fear
last_rejected.source_quote: cum martyres non ea metuentes magna fortitudine paterentur
last_rejected.why: "non ea metuentes" = "not fearing these things," not "with no fear" as a general state. The English "endured them" is also slightly off—"paterentur" is passive, "were suffering/enduring," with "magna fortitudine" ablative of manner.
last_rejected.fix: while the martyrs, not fearing these things, endured with great courage
last_rejected.ruling: 'endured them with great courage and no fear' adequately renders 'magna fortitudine paterentur non ea metuentes'; 'no fear' captures 'non ea metuentes' sufficiently.

last_rejected.quote: because no opportunity was given to perform due rites for the saints' funerals
last_rejected.source_quote: quod nulla dabatur potestas sanctorum funeribus iusta persoluere
last_rejected.why: "iusta persoluere" = "to pay due rites/dues," but "funeribus" is dative with "iusta"—"due rites for the funerals" or "burials." The English "perform due rites for the saints' funerals" is close but "iusta" as noun = "due rites, funeral rites."
last_rejected.fix: because no power was given to pay the due rites for the saints' burials
last_rejected.ruling: 'perform due rites for the saints' funerals' correctly renders 'sanctorum funeribus iusta persoluere'; 'iusta' as rites is standard.

last_rejected.quote: because they themselves in some way felt for those who felt nothing at all
last_rejected.source_quote: quia in nullo modo sentientibus ipsi quodam modo sentiebant
last_rejected.why: "in nullo modo sentientibus" = "for those in no way feeling/sensing," dative of reference. The English "felt for" suggests compassion/empathy, but the Latin "sentiebant" is more literal: "they themselves in some way felt/sensed for those who in no way felt." The paradox is stronger in the Latin.
last_rejected.fix: because they themselves in some way felt for those who in no way felt
last_rejected.ruling: 'felt for those who felt nothing' captures the paradox of 'sentiebant/sentientibus'; 'felt for' works as both sense and compassion here.
